title: Results and Analysis
introduction: This chapter presents experimental results from evaluating the three optimized models on the NSL-KDD test set (22,544 samples).

sections.title: Comparative Performance Analysis
sections.content_html: Table 3.1 presents comprehensive metrics. Ensemble_Bagging achieves highest scores (91.60% balanced accuracy, 0.8244 MCC), followed by DecisionTree (91.19%, 0.8160 MCC). Ridge substantially underperforms (79.18%, 0.5894 MCC). McNemar's test confirms statistical significance (p < 0.001).

tables.caption: Comprehensive Accuracy Metrics Comparison
tables.description: This table reveals a clear performance hierarchy among the three model families. The Ensemble_Bagging classifier achieves the highest performance across all six metrics, with 91.60% balanced accuracy and MCC of 0.8244 indicating excellent classification capability. The NonLinear_DecisionTree follows closely with 91.19% balanced accuracy and 0.8160 MCC. Both non-linear methods achieve MCC values above 0.8, indicating strong correlation between predictions and true labels. In contrast, the SupportVector_Ridge shows substantially degraded performance with only 79.18% balanced accuracy and 0.5894 MCC, representing a fundamental limitation of linear classifiers for this problem domain.

figures.caption: Visual comparison of all evaluation metrics across models
figures.description: This grouped bar chart visualizes all six evaluation metrics for the three models. The visual pattern immediately reveals the performance stratification: Ensemble_Bagging and NonLinear_DecisionTree bars are nearly identical in height across all metrics, both substantially taller than SupportVector_Ridge bars. This confirms the performance gap between non-linear and linear methods is consistent across accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1-score, precision, recall, and MCC—not an artifact of any single metric choice.

figures.caption: Balanced Accuracy comparison
figures.description: This bar chart focuses on balanced accuracy—the arithmetic mean of sensitivity and specificity. This metric is particularly appropriate for intrusion detection as it gives equal weight to detecting attacks and correctly classifying normal traffic. The chart shows Ensemble_Bagging at 91.60%, DecisionTree at 91.19%, and Ridge at only 79.18%. The 12.42 percentage point gap between Ensemble and Ridge quantifies the cost of using a linear classifier for this non-linear classification problem.

figures.caption: Matthews Correlation Coefficient comparison
figures.description: This figure displays Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) for each model. MCC is considered one of the most reliable metrics for binary classification because it uses all four confusion matrix quadrants and produces a balanced measure even when classes are imbalanced. The Ensemble_Bagging achieves 0.8244, indicating excellent classification quality. The DecisionTree's 0.8160 MCC is statistically comparable. However, Ridge's 0.5894 MCC indicates only moderate correlation—substantially degraded classification quality unacceptable for production intrusion detection.

sections.title: Cross-Validation Results
sections.content_html: Five-fold stratified cross-validation assessed model stability. Low standard deviations (< 0.4%) indicate stable performance across data partitions.

tables.caption: 5-Fold Cross-Validation Results
tables.description: This table presents cross-validation performance metrics with standard deviations across five folds. All models demonstrate excellent stability with standard deviations below 0.4%. The Ensemble_Bagging achieves 95.21% CV balanced accuracy with only 0.21% variation, indicating highly consistent predictions. The DecisionTree shows slightly higher variance (0.30-0.31%) but remains very stable. The tight confidence intervals confirm that reported performance differences are statistically significant and not artifacts of particular data splits.

figures.caption: Cross-validation performance with error bars
figures.description: This figure visualizes cross-validation results with error bars representing standard deviation across five folds. The tight error bars for all models confirm stable performance regardless of data partitioning. Ensemble_Bagging shows the smallest error bars, consistent with ensemble methods' theoretical property of reducing variance through averaging. The consistent gap between non-linear methods (~95%) and linear Ridge (~81%) across all folds confirms this performance difference is fundamental rather than data-dependent.

sections.title: Bias-Variance Decomposition
sections.content_html: Bootstrap-based decomposition characterized error sources. Ensemble achieves optimal balance; DecisionTree has lowest bias but higher variance; Ridge shows severe underfitting (bias = 0.227).

tables.caption: Bias-Variance Decomposition
tables.description: This table presents bias-variance decomposition results from bootstrap analysis. The Ensemble_Bagging achieves optimal error composition with 12.1% bias and 2.7% variance, confirming bootstrap aggregating successfully reduces prediction variance. The DecisionTree shows lowest bias (8.8%) indicating its flexible decision boundaries most accurately capture the true classification function, but higher variance (3.4%) reflects sensitivity to training data. The Ridge classifier exhibits dramatically different profile: 22.7% bias dominates its error while variance is negligible (0.4%)—characteristic of underfitting where the linear model systematically misclassifies instances.

figures.caption: Bias-variance decomposition visualization
figures.description: This grouped bar chart visualizes bias-variance decomposition, showing bias, variance, and expected loss for each model. For Ensemble_Bagging and DecisionTree, expected loss bars are similar (~10-11%) with bias contributing the larger portion. For Ridge, the expected loss bar is dramatically taller (~23%), almost entirely composed of bias with minimal variance. This definitively establishes that Ridge's poor performance stems from underfitting—increasing model complexity cannot help because the fundamental problem is insufficient model expressiveness.

sections.title: Attack Detection Performance
sections.content_html: Ensemble achieves 87.20% detection rate with only 4.00% false alarms. Ridge detects only 65.36% of attacks while generating 7.00% false alarms.

tables.caption: Attack Detection Performance
tables.description: This table presents metrics specifically relevant to intrusion detection deployment. The Attack Detection Rate measures proportion of actual attacks correctly identified—critical for security where missed attacks have severe consequences. Ensemble_Bagging detects 87.20% of attacks, meaning 11,191 of 12,833 test set attacks are correctly flagged. Ridge detects only 65.36%—missing 4,445 intrusions that would proceed undetected. The False Alarm Rate shows Ensemble's 4.00% (388 false alerts) versus Ridge's 7.00% (680 false positives), meaning Ridge generates 75% more false alarms while detecting far fewer attacks.

figures.caption: Detection Rate vs. False Alarm Rate
figures.description: This scatter plot shows Detection Rate against False Alarm Rate, visualizing the accuracy-alarm tradeoff. The ideal position is upper-left: high detection with low false alarms. Ensemble_Bagging and DecisionTree occupy this desirable region with detection rates above 86% and false alarm rates below 5%. Ridge appears in clearly inferior position: lower detection and more false alarms. This encapsulates operational reality: deploying Ridge would result in missing over one-third of attacks while handling 75% more false alerts.

figures.caption: Precision-Recall comparison
figures.description: This figure compares precision and recall metrics across all models. High precision indicates that when a model flags an attack, it is usually correct. High recall indicates the model catches most actual attacks. Both non-linear methods achieve excellent balance of precision (>96%) and recall (>86%), while Ridge shows degraded recall (65%) despite acceptable precision (92.5%). This asymmetric performance makes Ridge unsuitable for security applications where missing attacks is more costly than false alarms.

sections.title: Confusion Matrix Analysis
sections.content_html: Ensemble correctly detects 11,191 attacks while missing 1,642; Ridge misses 4,445 attacks—2,803 additional undetected intrusions.

tables.caption: Confusion Matrix Values
tables.description: This table presents raw confusion matrix values revealing practical implications of performance differences. Ensemble_Bagging correctly identifies 11,191 of 12,833 attacks (True Positives) while misclassifying 1,642 attacks as normal (False Negatives) and generating 388 false alerts (False Positives). Ridge's confusion matrix shows only 8,388 True Positives—4,445 attacks go undetected, 2,803 more missed attacks than Ensemble. From a security perspective, these additional undetected intrusions could include data breaches, malware installations, or reconnaissance activities proceeding without alerting defenders.

figures.caption: Confusion matrices for all models
figures.description: This figure displays confusion matrices for all three models using color-coded heatmaps. Darker colors indicate higher values. Ensemble and DecisionTree matrices appear nearly identical with dark cells in True Positive (upper-left) and True Negative (lower-right) positions. Ridge matrix shows noticeably lighter True Positive cell and darker False Negative cell, visually confirming its attack detection deficiency. The diagonal dominance in non-linear methods indicates accurate classification of both classes.

figures.caption: Performance metrics heatmap
figures.description: This heatmap provides a comprehensive visualization of all performance metrics across the three models. Color intensity represents metric values, with darker colors indicating better performance. The heatmap clearly shows Ensemble_Bagging and DecisionTree with consistently dark cells across all metrics, while Ridge shows noticeably lighter cells, particularly for recall and MCC. This visualization enables quick identification of each model's strengths and weaknesses across multiple evaluation dimensions.

sections.title: ROC-AUC Analysis
sections.content_html: Ensemble AUC = 0.9642, DecisionTree AUC = 0.9589, Ridge AUC = 0.8734. DeLong's test confirms significant differences (p < 0.001).

tables.caption: ROC-AUC Scores with Confidence Intervals
tables.description: This table presents ROC-AUC scores with 95% confidence intervals computed using DeLong's method. AUC values above 0.9 indicate excellent discrimination; 0.8-0.9 indicates good discrimination. Both non-linear methods achieve excellent AUC (>0.95), while Ridge achieves only good discrimination (0.87). The tight confidence intervals (±0.003 to ±0.006) confirm reliable estimates. The 0.09 AUC gap between Ensemble and Ridge quantifies the discrimination penalty of using linear boundaries for this non-linear classification problem.

figures.caption: ROC curves for all models
figures.description: This figure displays ROC curves for all three models, plotting True Positive Rate against False Positive Rate across classification thresholds. Curves closer to the upper-left corner indicate better discrimination. Ensemble_Bagging and DecisionTree curves nearly overlap, both hugging the upper-left corner, indicating excellent discrimination ability. Ridge's curve is noticeably lower, reflecting its reduced ability to separate attack and normal traffic across different threshold settings.

sections.title: Generalization and Training Analysis
sections.content_html: Generalization gap: Ensemble 3.61%, DecisionTree 3.55%, Ridge 1.50%. Ridge's smaller gap reflects limited learning capacity rather than superior generalization.

tables.caption: Generalization Gap Analysis
tables.description: This table quantifies the generalization gap—difference between cross-validation and test set performance. Ensemble_Bagging drops 3.61 percentage points from 95.21% to 91.60%; DecisionTree drops 3.55 points. These similar gaps suggest both models learn equally generalizable patterns. Ridge's smaller gap (1.50 points) appears favorable but is misleading: Ridge starts from lower baseline and has less room to degrade. More fundamentally, Ridge's limited capacity means it cannot capture complex patterns—there is little specialized knowledge to lose when facing novel attacks.

figures.caption: Training vs. test performance comparison
figures.description: This figure uses grouped bars to compare cross-validation (training) and test performance. Each model has two adjacent bars—taller representing CV performance and shorter representing test performance. The gap between bars visualizes generalization penalty. For Ensemble and DecisionTree, both bars are tall with similar gaps indicating strong performance that degrades modestly with novel attacks. For Ridge, both bars are shorter—its smaller gap is not a virtue, both bars are simply lower on the chart.

figures.caption: Training time comparison
figures.description: This bar chart compares training times across models. Ensemble_Bagging requires 79.41 seconds—substantially longer due to training 150 individual decision trees. DecisionTree completes in only 0.87 seconds, nearly 100 times faster. Ridge is fastest at 0.38 seconds with its closed-form solution. However, training time should not drive model selection: all times are under 2 minutes and training is a one-time cost. The critical question is whether Ensemble's training investment is justified by its marginal accuracy advantage.

figures.caption: Radar chart of model performance
figures.description: This radar chart provides multi-dimensional visualization of model performance across all key metrics. Each axis represents a different metric, and the area covered by each model's polygon indicates overall performance. Ensemble_Bagging and DecisionTree show large, nearly overlapping polygons covering most of the chart area. Ridge's polygon is noticeably smaller, particularly contracted along the recall and MCC axes, providing an intuitive summary of its performance limitations.

figures.caption: Feature importance comparison
figures.description: This figure compares feature importance rankings across tree-based models. Content-based features (src_bytes, dst_bytes) consistently rank highest, indicating byte transfer patterns are key discriminators between normal and attack traffic. Traffic features (count, same_srv_rate) rank second, capturing connection frequency patterns. This consistency across models suggests these features capture genuine signal rather than model-specific artifacts, providing guidance for feature engineering in future IDS development.

figures.caption: Performance by attack category
figures.description: This figure breaks down detection performance across the four NSL-KDD attack categories: DoS, Probe, R2L, and U2R. All models perform best on DoS attacks (highest volume in training data) and worst on U2R attacks (rarest category). Non-linear methods maintain substantial advantages across all categories, with the gap most pronounced for subtle R2L and U2R attacks that require complex pattern recognition beyond linear classifier capabilities.

sections.title: Summary
sections.content_html:
Key Findings:

  1. Ensemble and tree methods achieve 91%+ balanced accuracy with MCC > 0.8
  2. Linear methods severely underfit (79% balanced accuracy, 0.59 MCC)
  3. Non-linear methods detect 87% of attacks with 4% false alarms vs. Ridge's 65%/7%
  4. Bias-variance analysis confirms Ridge's high irreducible bias (0.227)

Recommendation: Ensemble or tree-based methods strongly preferred for intrusion detection.
